questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on his glans penis, with a clean base and indurated edges, for 3 weeks. Regional lymph nodes are enlarged and non-tender. Darkfield microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spirochetes. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: This is primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre). Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the drug of choice for primary and secondary syphilis. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a vegetating plaque on the dorsum of the foot with multiple sinuses discharging yellow 'sulfur granules'. Microscopy shows branching gram-positive filaments. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Yellow granules in mycetoma most commonly indicate Actinomadura madurae (actinomycetoma). White granules suggest Actinomadura pelletieri or Streptomyces, while black granules indicate eumycetoma. The foot location and occupation support Madura foot.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with grouped vesicles along a dermatomal distribution on the chest, accompanied by severe burning pain. Two days later, the lesions become pustular and some cross the midline. The most appropriate antiviral therapy is:
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg five times daily for 7 days
Valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 500 mg three times daily for 7 days
Acyclovir IV 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7–10 days
questions.exp: Disseminated herpes zoster (crossing midline, immunocompromised host) warrants IV acyclovir due to risk of visceral dissemination and encephalitis. Oral antivirals are insufficient for disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with erythematous, scaly plaques with well-defined borders on her forearms, worsening in winter. She has a family history of psoriasis. Histopathology shows parakeratosis, absence of granular layer, elongated rete ridges, and suprapapillary thinning with dilated capillaries. Which finding is pathognomonic?
questions.exp: Munro's microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum) and Kogoj's spongiform pustules (neutrophils in stratum spinosum/Malpighi) are both pathognomonic for psoriasis. Pautrier's microabscesses are seen in mycosis fungoides.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple painless, flesh-coloured, umbilicated papules on the face and neck. CD4 count is 75 cells/mm³. The organism responsible belongs to which family?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the Poxviridae family. In HIV patients, widespread facial involvement is common when CD4 count drops below 100.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches over the trunk and extremities. Slit-skin smear is negative. Biopsy shows granulomas along nerve bundles in the dermis with no AFB. Lepromin test is strongly positive (+3). What is the classification of this patient's leprosy?
questions.exp: TT leprosy: few (1–2) well-defined hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, negative smear, strongly positive lepromin test (>5mm), granulomas with lymphocytes around nerves, no AFB. BT has more lesions and may have a weakly positive lepromin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male on long-term dapsone therapy for leprosy presents with sudden-onset haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia. Which enzyme deficiency makes this side effect more severe?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in all patients to some degree, but G6PD-deficient patients are at much greater risk of severe haemolysis because they cannot regenerate NADPH to protect red cells from oxidative stress.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, sparing mucosae. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF. The autoantigens are BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1), hemidesmosomal proteins.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with flaccid bullae on the trunk, which rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG deposition in an intercellular 'fish-net' pattern throughout the epidermis. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (mucosal and cutaneous) is caused by antibodies against both desmoglein 3 (mucosa) and desmoglein 1 (skin). The DIF shows intercellular 'fish-net' IgG. Pemphigus foliaceus targets only Dsg1.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman with SLE presents with malar erythema, photosensitivity, discoid plaques, and a positive ANA titre of 1:640 with anti-dsDNA antibodies. The antibody most specific for SLE-associated nephritis is:
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis, and titres often rise before renal flares. Anti-Sm is highly specific for SLE but does not correlate with nephritis. Anti-histone is seen in drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening of the fingers and face, telangiectasias, and dysphagia. HRCT chest shows basilar fibrosis. Serological test shows anti-centromere antibody. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CREST (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is the limited form of SSc. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc/CREST. Diffuse SSc is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectatic vessels and central ulceration on the nose. He has a long history of sun exposure. Histology shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact. The most common site for this tumour is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy. The most common site is the head and neck, and specifically the lower eyelid is the most frequent periorbital site. Nose is a very common overall site, but lower eyelid leads periorbital involvement.

questions.q: A 35-year-old fair-skinned man presents with an irregularly pigmented lesion on his back. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, irregular dots and globules, blue-white veil, and regression structures. Biopsy reveals malignant melanocytes at the DEJ extending into the superficial dermis. Breslow thickness is 0.8 mm with no ulceration. The recommended surgical margin is:
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness ≤1 mm (without ulceration/high mitotic rate), wide local excision with 1 cm margin is recommended. Margins increase to 1–2 cm for 1–2 mm thickness and 2 cm for >2 mm thickness.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne wants to start a pregnancy. When should isotretinoin be stopped before attempting conception?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic (Pregnancy Category X). The iPLEDGE programme requires stopping isotretinoin and waiting at least 1 month before attempting conception, confirmed by two negative pregnancy tests. The standard answer tested in Indian DNB/MD exams is 1 month washout before conception.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks gestation presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques on her abdomen, sparing the periumbilical area. DIF of perilesional skin is negative. This condition is best described as:
questions.exp: PUPPP (Polymorphic Eruption of Pregnancy) classically starts within abdominal striae and spares the periumbilical area, unlike pemphigoid gestationis which begins periumbilically. DIF is negative in PUPPP. It is the most common specific dermatosis of pregnancy.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with thickening of the lateral nail fold with yellowish-brown discolouration and transverse ridging of the nail plate. Subungual hyperkeratosis is noted. KOH examination of subungual debris shows hyphae. Which organism is the most common cause of distal subungual onychomycosis?
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common dermatophyte causing onychomycosis worldwide, typically presenting as distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO). T. mentagrophytes is the second most common, often causing white superficial onychomycosis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with chronic vegetating plaques with a verrucous surface on the lower leg following a splinter injury 2 years ago. Biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and pigmented fungal cells ('copper penny' bodies) in the epidermis. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous plaques and 'Medlar bodies' (copper-penny/sclerotic cells), which are brown, thick-walled muriform cells. Fonsecaea pedrosoi is the most common causative agent. Sporothrix causes lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with pruritic papules in the finger webs, wrists, and waist. She mentions her family members have similar symptoms. Dermoscopy reveals the 'delta-wing jet with contrail' sign. The treatment of choice for the entire household is:
opts: Topical permethrin 5% applied overnight to the whole body, repeated after 1 week
Topical benzyl benzoate 25% applied for 3 consecutive nights
questions.exp: Scabies treatment of choice is permethrin 5% cream, applied from neck down for 8–12 hours, repeated after 1 week. All household and close contacts must be treated simultaneously. Oral ivermectin is an alternative, especially for crusted scabies or large outbreaks.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which treatment is most appropriate for localised disease?
questions.exp: Impetigo with localised lesions (≤5 lesions) is best treated with topical mupirocin 2% ointment, which is bactericidal against S. aureus and Streptococcus. Systemic antibiotics are indicated for extensive disease, systemic symptoms, or MRSA infection.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with extensive psoriasis is being considered for biologic therapy. He has latent tuberculosis detected on IGRA testing. Which biologic is relatively contraindicated and requires most caution regarding TB reactivation?
questions.exp: TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) carry the highest risk of TB reactivation because TNF-alpha is critical for granuloma formation and containment of M. tuberculosis. Mandatory TB screening and chemoprophylaxis are required before initiation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with generalised lymphadenopathy, fever, sore throat, morbilliform rash after ampicillin, and splenomegaly. Paul-Bunnell test is positive. Which virus is responsible?
questions.exp: This is infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV (HHV-4). Characteristic features include pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytosis, ampicillin rash, and positive heterophile antibody test (Paul-Bunnell/Monospot). CMV can cause a similar syndrome but heterophile antibody is negative.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a solitary anogenital wart (condyloma acuminata). On acetowhitening, the lesion turns white. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible?
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) are caused predominantly by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types responsible for cervical, vulvar, penile, and anal carcinomas.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules with Wickham's striae on the flexor surface of the wrists. Oral mucosa shows reticular white lace-like pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus is characterised by the '5 Ps': Purple, Polygonal, Pruritic, Planar (flat-topped) Papules. Wickham's striae (white reticulate lines) are pathognomonic. Oral involvement with reticular white plaques is common. Histology shows saw-tooth rete ridges and band-like lichenoid infiltrate.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with widespread erythema, skin tenderness, and large, flaccid bullae that rupture leaving scalded-appearing skin. Nikolsky sign is positive. Blood culture grows S. aureus producing exfoliative toxin. DIF of skin is negative. The toxin responsible cleaves:
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (serine proteases) produced by phage group 2 S. aureus. These toxins specifically cleave desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, causing superficial blistering, similar to pemphigus foliaceus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a well-circumscribed, pearly white dermal plaque on the neck. On dermoscopy, comma-shaped vessels are seen. Biopsy shows a proliferation of spindle cells with whorled pattern and tactoid bodies (encapsulated nerve bundles). The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Neurofibroma: benign peripheral nerve sheath tumour showing spindle cells in a myxoid stroma with Wagner-Meissner (tactoid) bodies. Solitary neurofibromas are typically sporadic. Multiple neurofibromas in a young patient suggest neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). DFSP shows storiform pattern and CD34 positivity.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with depigmented patches on the face and hands. Wood's lamp examination shows milk-white fluorescence with sharp borders. Melanocytes are absent on histology. Which treatment modality is most effective for generalised vitiligo involving >30% BSA?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB, 311–312 nm) is the gold standard for generalised vitiligo (>10–15% BSA). It has a superior safety profile compared to PUVA and does not require photosensitiser. NB-UVB induces melanocyte migration from follicular reservoirs.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with diffuse non-scarring alopecia with positive hair pull test. Trichoscopy shows 'exclamation mark hairs' and yellow dots (empty follicles). The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Alopecia areata trichoscopy: yellow dots (follicular infundibulum filled with keratin/sebum), black dots (cadaverised hairs), 'exclamation mark hairs' (tapered proximal shaft), and short vellus hairs. Trichotillomania shows coiled/broken hairs without yellow dots.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male is undergoing patch testing. A reading at 48 hours shows a papular erythematous reaction at the test site that is still present (and increases) at 96 hours. This is classified as:
questions.exp: ICDRG patch test reading: + (weak positive): non-vesicular erythema, infiltration, possibly papules; ++ (strong positive): vesicles; +++ (extreme positive): bullous reaction. An irritant reaction typically fades by 96h. A true allergic (+) reaction increases over time due to T-cell–mediated Type IV hypersensitivity.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with a violaceous, indurated plaque on the lower leg persisting for years after a traumatic injury. Biopsy shows a dense band-like infiltrate with atypical lymphocytes (CD4+, CD8-) and epidermotropism forming clusters (Pautrier's microabscesses). The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Hallmarks include epidermotropism, Pautrier's microabscesses (intraepidermal clusters of atypical lymphocytes), CD4+ T-cell phenotype, and cerebriform nuclei. It progresses through patch → plaque → tumour stages.

questions.q: A 33-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer over the genitalia with an undermined, oedematous, serpiginous edge and a dirty necrotic base. Adjacent satellite ulcers are present. The causative organism grows as 'school of fish' pattern on Gram stain. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chancroid: caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative coccobacillus that shows the characteristic 'school of fish' / 'railroad track' arrangement on Gram stain. Ulcer is painful with soft, ragged, undermined edges. Treatment is azithromycin 1 g single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM.

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic woman presents with cellulitis of the lower leg unresponsive to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5 days. Wound swab shows MRSA. The antibiotic of choice for inpatient treatment of MRSA skin and soft tissue infection is:
questions.exp: Vancomycin IV is the drug of choice for serious MRSA infections including cellulitis requiring hospitalisation. Linezolid and daptomycin are alternatives. TMP-SMX is used for outpatient MRSA SSTI. Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant in pulmonary infections but is effective for SSTI.
